summary: Compare the main phone answering options and pick the one that fits your restaurant and budget.
intro:
A restaurant phone answering service can be a human service, an AI phone host, voicemail, or call forwarding to your own staff. The right choice depends on your call volume, how often calls turn into orders, and whether you want a fixed monthly bill or pay only when an order is completed.

For a pizza shop, deli, or family restaurant, the big question is simple: do you want someone to answer, take the order, and send it to the kitchen, or just catch messages? ROAL is one option in that mix: it answers calls, takes pickup and delivery orders from your live menu, and sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen.

sections.h2: What are the main restaurant phone answering service options?
sections.body:
For most restaurants, the choices are pretty narrow. Here is the practical version:

| Option | What it does | Best for | Main tradeoff |
|---|---|---|---|
| Human answering service | A person answers and relays messages or takes orders | Busy shops that want a live person | Usually billed per minute or per call |
| AI phone host | Answers, takes orders, handles common questions | Restaurants that want order capture without hiring more staff | Some calls still need staff help |
| Voicemail | Caller leaves a message | Very low call volume | Missed orders and slow callbacks |
| Call forwarding to staff | Rings your team instead of going to voicemail | Small teams with room to answer | Staff gets pulled away from the counter |

A useful phone script for any option is: "Thanks for calling. If you’d like pickup, please have your order ready. If you have a question about hours or the menu, I can help." That script keeps the call moving and sets expectations fast.

If you use ROAL, it can answer hours, address, parking, and menu questions, and it can take pickup and delivery orders from the restaurant’s live menu. Tricky calls like catering, complaints, allergy-sensitive questions, and manager requests still go to staff with a summary.

sections.h2: How do human answering services compare on cost?
sections.body:
Human answering services are often the most familiar option, but they are usually billed per minute or per call. That makes them flexible, but it can get expensive if your phone rings a lot.

Here is a simple way to think about it:

1. Estimate your monthly call volume.
2. Estimate how many of those calls are actual orders.
3. Multiply by the service’s minute or call rate.
4. Compare that total to what you already spend on labor.

Worked example: say you get 300 calls a month and 120 of them are order calls. If a human service charges by the minute or by the call, your bill will move with every extra call, even the short ones. Plug in your own number from your past phone log and see what the total looks like.

This is where an AI phone host can feel different. ROAL bills $0.90 per completed phone order, meaning a confirmed order whose ticket reached the kitchen screen. There is no monthly fee, no setup fee, no per-minute fee, and no contract. Calls, questions, and test calls are unlimited and free.

sections.h2: When does a monthly AI phone plan make sense?
sections.body:
Many AI phone tools for restaurants charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often roughly $79 to $599, whether or not orders come in. That can make sense if you want predictable billing and a lot of phone coverage every day.

A simple comparison table helps:

| Plan style | Your bill pattern | Good fit |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed monthly fee | Same charge every month | Restaurants with steady call volume |
| Pay per completed order | Bill only when an order is confirmed | Shops with uneven traffic or seasonal swings |

If you want a quick check, use your average order value. Say a $28 average order. Then ask: is a fixed monthly fee worth it if the phone only produces a handful of orders on slow weeks? You can also compare a pay-per-order model to fixed pricing with the [pay per order vs monthly AI phone plans](/compare/monthly-ai-phone-plans) page.

ROAL is built for this pay-only-when-it-works approach. The owner pastes a website, Google Maps link, or name and city at /try, test-calls the host in the browser, and can go live without a sign-up during setup.

sections.h2: What happens if I forward my restaurant number?
sections.body:
If you choose forwarding, the restaurant keeps its own number. ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and you forward your existing number to it.

Here is the basic setup flow:

1. Claim the host.
2. Keep your current restaurant number.
3. Forward all calls, or only busy/unanswered calls.
4. Test with a real call.
5. Turn forwarding off any time if you want to switch back.

The exact codes depend on your carrier and plan, so always confirm with your phone company and test after you set it up. On many landlines and some carriers, *72 starts call forwarding and *73 turns it off. On some mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off. Busy and unanswered call codes can vary too.

A practical script for the team is: "We still keep our main number. Calls now route through the host when we’re busy, and we can switch it off any time." That helps staff understand the change before the first rush.

sections.h2: What should the phone host actually handle?
sections.body:
The best restaurant phone answering service is the one that handles the calls that steal the most time. That usually means order-taking and the common questions that come in all day.

A phone host should be able to handle:

- Items, sizes, modifiers, and notes
- Caller name and phone number
- Ready time quotes
- Order confirmation back to the caller
- Language matching when possible
- Reservation requests
- Menu, hours, address, and parking questions

It should also know when to stop. For example: "I can help with pickup orders and menu questions. For catering, allergy-sensitive questions, or a manager request, I’ll send this to the team." That kind of handoff protects the guest and your staff.

ROAL also avoids a common problem: it does not offer items marked sold out. And it never takes card numbers over the phone; payment happens at pickup or however the restaurant already takes it. That keeps the call focused on getting the order right and getting it to the kitchen.

sections.h2: How do I compare phone answering options for my restaurant?
sections.body:
Use the same four questions for every option so you are comparing apples to apples.

- Does it answer during the rush, after hours, and when staff are tied up?
- Does it take real orders, or only messages?
- Does it help with menu questions, or dump those calls on the team?
- Does the pricing match your call volume?

A quick owner checklist:

1. Pull your last 2 weeks of call volume.
2. Count how many calls were orders, questions, or anything else.
3. Decide what you want automated first: orders, FAQs, or both.
4. Check whether the pricing is per call, per minute, per month, or per completed order.
5. Test the setup before your next rush.

If you want to see how a modern option looks in practice, ROAL’s dashboard includes live kitchen tickets, call history with transcripts and recordings, a menu editor, hours, FAQs, upsell suggestions, and multi-location menus. You can also compare formats on the [AI phone host vs answering service](/compare/answering-service) and [AI phone host vs hiring phone staff](/compare/hiring-phone-staff) pages.

A soft starting point is to [Build a free test host](/try) from your website, Google Maps link, or menu file, then call it yourself before you decide.

takeaways: Human answering services are usually billed per minute or per call, so costs move with call volume.
Many monthly AI phone plans charge even when no orders come in, often around $79 to $599 per location.
ROAL uses pay-per-completed-order pricing: $0.90 for a confirmed order that reaches the kitchen screen.
The best option depends on whether you want order capture, menu help, or just message taking.
Always test forwarding with a real call before you rely on it during a rush.

faq.q: What is the cheapest restaurant phone answering service option?
faq.a: The cheapest option depends on how many orders you actually complete. Voicemail is cheapest upfront, but it can cost you orders if people hang up. If you want a service that answers and captures real orders, compare per-minute, per-call, monthly, and per-completed-order pricing against your own call log.

faq.q: Should I use call forwarding or a phone answering service for my restaurant?
faq.a: Use call forwarding if your staff can still answer the phone without hurting the counter or kitchen. Use a phone answering service if calls are frequent and the team cannot keep up. Forwarding keeps things simple, but it can still pull staff away from guests and prep work.

faq.q: Can an AI phone host take pickup and delivery orders for a restaurant?
faq.a: Yes, a restaurant-focused AI phone host can take pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, collect name and phone number, quote a ready time, and confirm the order back. ROAL also sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It does not take card numbers over the phone.

faq.a: Setup depends on your carrier and phone system. On many landlines and some carriers, *72 forwards all calls and *73 turns it off; on some mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off. Codes vary, so confirm with your carrier and test with a real call before peak hours.
